title: External sandboxes for coding agents
summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents 

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

 I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects .

 My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

 To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

 external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.

 external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.

 external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

 Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

 The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without s
title_zh: External sandboxes for coding agents

title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
summary:
Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive.

 Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first?

 Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential.

 This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead
title_zh: Can AI help build a healthier future?

title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
summary:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

 You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io :

 Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script

 Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI

 Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository

 Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette

 Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

 The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

 As an example, consider the following URL:

 https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

 We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . 

 In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. 

 “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” 

 Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” 

 However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce.

title: llm 0.37.3
summary:
Release: llm 0.37.3 

 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

 Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code .

 Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

 select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
 
 Returns this:

 {"a":[1]}
 
 But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

 {"a":"[1]"}
 
 According to D. Richard Hipp :

 That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

 The workaround looks like this:

 select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

 Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
summary:
At a glance 

 Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.

 TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.

 Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.

 AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. 

 In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Securi
title_zh: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient

title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
summary:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.
 Subscribe now 
 AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:
 …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…
 Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”
 Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.
